description: Nether Nebula is a team of passionate innovators exploring the mysteries of the universe through technology and science. For NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we aim to build an interactive platform that visualizes astronomical data, compares sky observations over time, and helps identify moving celestial objects using AI and image processing. Our vision is to make space exploration accessible and turn cosmic data into discoveries.
summary:
SPHEREx ChronoSky is an interactive 3D web app and validation-first moving-object discovery workbench for the NASA Hackathon. It analyzes multi-epoch SPHEREx near-infrared data (0.75–5.0 μm, six LVF bands, R=35–128) to find asteroids, Centaurs, TNOs and interstellar visitors — without claiming Planet Nine discovery.

Three Hero Moments: (1) Credibility — SkyBoT known-object recovery, synthetic completeness heatmaps, 200-trial time-scrambled null test for false-alarm rates; (2) Motion-Corrected LVF Spectroscopy — shifting extraction apertures along predicted trajectories at each timestamp, using WCS-WAVE (key="W", sip=None) after IMAGE−ZODI subtraction, un-smearing spectra; (3) Serendipity & Devil's Advocate — IsolationForest ranking, five artifact falsification probabilities, SHA-256 evidence cards, Blink Quest human learning.

Five missions extend it: Approach Navigator, Interstellar Object Hunter (hyperbolic e≥1 via vis-viva), Icy Ocean World Spectroscopist, Multi-Survey Consensus (ZTF+TESS+NEOWISE), Active Learning. Suspect targets include Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855. Built on 12 modular Python engines (FastAPI, Three.js) with dual-mode MongoDB/JSON storage and an offline cached benchmark. Sources: IRSA SIA v2, SkyBoT, MPC, Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, NEOWISE, Pan-STARRS, ZTF, TESS.
details:
[What It Does & How It Works

SPHEREx ChronoSky is a validation-first moving-object discovery workbench that turns multi-epoch NASA/IPAC SPHEREx infrared observations into an interactive 3D research platform. Rather than immediately hunting for anomalies, it first proves the pipeline is trustworthy.]

The pipeline operates in four stages:

1. Query — SPHERExClient queries the IRSA SIA v2 API for SPHEREx observations (Wide/Deep collections) at a sky position and builds server-side cutout URLs.

2. Process — FITSProcessor reads the 6-extension Level 2 MEF (IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE, ZODI, PSF, WCS-WAVE). ImageProcessor subtracts ZODI, masks bad FLAGS bits, reprojects to a common frame, and computes inverse-variance ΔSNR difference images.

3. Detect — MovingObjectDetector links detections across epochs using a 3D KDTree, fits preliminary orbits, and estimates heliocentric distance as a 68% confidence interval [d_min, d_med, d_max] from solar-elongation parallax geometry (never a single false-precision AU).

4. Validate — PipelineValidator runs known-object recovery (SkyBoT), synthetic completeness grids, and a 200-trial time-scrambled null test to calibrate false-alarm rates and set promotion thresholds.

Three Hero Moments structure the interface:

- Hero 1 — Credibility & Coverage Lab: recall scorecards, completeness heatmaps ("what SPHEREx can rule out"), null-test FAR meter.

- Hero 2 — Motion-Corrected LVF Spectroscopy: because LVFs sample different wavelengths at different exposure times, a moving object's spectrum is smeared at fixed (RA, Dec). We shift the extraction aperture along the predicted trajectory at each exposure timestamp and evaluate WCS-WAVE (key="W", sip=None), reconstructing a clean 0.75–5.0 μm SED.

- Hero 3 — Serendipity Feed & Devil's Advocate: IsolationForest anomaly ranking, five falsification probabilities (cosmic ray, persistence, optical ghost, proper-motion star, zodiacal residual) plus genuine-mover probability, SHA-256 evidence cards, and human-in-the-loop Blink Quest voting.

Five missions extend the platform — Approach Navigator (3D Catmull-Rom trajectory + light-time stamps), Interstellar Object Hunter (vis-viva hyperbolic detection, e ≥ 1), Icy Ocean World Spectroscopist (layered ice classes), Multi-Survey Consensus (ZTF + TESS + NEOWISE), and Active Learning (uncertainty sampling).

Benefits:

- Scientifically honest — every candidate ships with a measured false-alarm rate and a quantitative artifact breakdown; no claim is made without the evidence to support it.

- Artifact-resistant — Devil's Advocate plus Gaia DR3 proper-motion cross-checks systematically suppress cosmic rays, persistence trails, ghosts, and fast stars before they reach a human.

- Spectroscopically correct — motion-corrected extraction recovers real ice features (H₂O, CH₄, CO₂, CO) that fixed-aperture photometry would smear away.

- Reproducible — SHA-256 hashes over canonicalized evidence records, plus standard exports (VOTable, 80-column MPC, CSV, JSON).

- Demo-proof — an offline cached benchmark means every Hero Moment runs instantly with no network dependency.

- Degradation-proof infrastructure — MongoDB Atlas 2dsphere in production, automatic SQLite/JSON fallback locally.

Intended Impact:

ChronoSky reframes the hackathon question from "can you find Planet Nine?" to "what can this dataset actually constrain or rule out?" That shift is the scientifically honest one. The deliverable is a reusable workbench: the same architecture that validates TNO candidates extends to interstellar visitors, icy-world characterization, and cross-survey consensus. Over time, this could become a community vetting layer for SPHEREx small-body science — with human Blink Quest labels continuously improving the detector.

Tools, Languages & Software:

- Languages: Python 3.14, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3, LaTeX

- Science/ML: astropy, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn (HistGradientBoosting, RandomForest, ExtraTrees, IsolationForest, VotingClassifier), photutils, reproject, pandas, matplotlib

- Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, asyncio continuous evaluator, requests

- Database: MongoDB Atlas (2dsphere geospatial) with SQLite/JSON fallback via pymongo

- Frontend: Three.js r158 (ACES filmic tone mapping, PBR materials, shadow maps, CatmullRomCurve3 trajectories), vanilla JS, Canvas 2D for spectra/heatmaps

- Data sources: IRSA SIA v2 & cutout service, IMCCE SkyBoT, MPC, Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, NEOWISE, Pan-STARRS, ZTF, TESS

- Hardware: standard laptop/desktop; no GPU required (GPU optional for WebGPU roadmap item)

Creativity:

- Validation-first framing — the team inverted the usual demo order: credibility is Hero 1, not an appendix.

- Motion-corrected LVF spectroscopy — treats the instrument's wavelength-position coupling as a bug to be corrected, not a limitation to be accepted.

- Interactive 3D encounter — the Approach Navigator turns a static distance estimate into a tangible "fly to the object" research experience with light-time stamps.

- Honest probabilistic presentation — a 68% distance interval and a six-way falsification breakdown instead of a triumphant single number.

- Human-in-the-loop design — Blink Quest is a first-class science instrument, not a gamification afterthought.

Factors Considered:

- Scientific integrity — a persistent disclaimer on every view and export; no "discovery" language for unconfirmed candidates.

- Judging-day reliability — offline cache, dual-mode storage, and no API keys required for IRSA.

- Reproducibility — strict inter-file data contracts, SHA-256 provenance, open-source stack.

- Security — all configuration (e.g., MONGODB_URI) loaded from .env; secrets never committed.

- Accessibility & usability — mobile-first responsive layout, WCAG-AA contrast, keyboard navigation, ARIA labels.

- Honest limitations — simulated benchmarks and mock motion-correction are documented explicitly, with an addressable roadmap.
